title: Satisfy Accessible Authentication and Identify Input Purpose in sign-in
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §2 lists the WCAG 2.2 criteria an ink app is most likely to fail, but it omits two AA criteria that are new in WCAG 2.2 and land squarely on our login flow: **3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)** and **1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose**. 3.3.8 forbids a cognitive function test (remembering, transcribing, or re-typing a code) in any authentication step unless an alternative or a mechanism to assist exists. Our phone-OTP flow ({{SN-AUTH-006}}, UI in {{SN-ONB-003}}) is exactly the pattern 3.3.8 targets: a six-digit code the user must memorise from an SMS and re-type into six separate boxes. 1.3.5 requires that fields collecting information about the user declare their purpose so autofill and symbol/icon substitution can assist. `accessibility.md` §10 only asks that the OTP input be labelled and the +91 prefix announced; it does not require paste, autofill, or password-manager support.

## Scope

**In:** OTP entry that accepts a full paste of the code into any cell and distributes it across the boxes; platform one-time-code autofill (iOS `textContentType = .oneTimeCode`, Android SMS Retriever / `autofillHints = smsOtpCode`, web `autocomplete="one-time-code" inputmode="numeric"`); password-manager and passkey-friendly markup on every identity field (phone, email, name) via the platform autofill hints and web `autocomplete` tokens (`tel`, `email`, `name`, `given-name`); never blocking paste on any credential or code field; a visible **Resend code** path with the remaining-time announced; a documented 3.3.8 argument for each sign-in method (OIDC providers delegate the test to the IdP, which is permitted).

**Out:** the OTP transport and rate limiting ({{SN-AUTH-006}}), passkey support as a feature, biometric app lock ({{SN-AUTH-014}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pasting a 6-digit code into the first OTP cell fills all six and submits; paste is never intercepted or stripped on any platform.
- [ ] iOS QuickType offers the code from the SMS; Android autofills through SMS Retriever; Chrome/Safari on web offer the WebOTP or autocomplete suggestion.
- [ ] Every identity field declares an input purpose (autofill hint / `autocomplete` token) verified in a snapshot test of the field configuration.
- [ ] No authentication step requires transcription or memorisation without an assisting mechanism; the reasoning is recorded per method in `docs/design/accessibility-conformance.md`.
- [ ] Screen readers announce the field purpose, the code length, remaining resend time, and any error as text (not colour).
- [ ] Keyboard and switch users can complete sign-in end to end without a mouse or gesture.

## Technical notes

OTP cells should be one logical text field rendered as six cells rather than six `TextField`s, so paste, autofill, and screen-reader value reporting work; if six fields are kept, implement a paste handler that splits the clipboard and moves focus. Flutter: `autofillHints: [AutofillHints.oneTimeCode]` inside an `AutofillGroup`; web needs the `autocomplete` attribute to reach the DOM input Flutter web creates. Wire the same hints in {{SN-ONB-002}} method buttons for provider sign-in.

## Security & privacy

Paste support does not weaken OTP security — rate limiting and expiry ({{SN-AUTH-006}}) are the control. Do not log clipboard contents or autofilled values. SMS Retriever avoids requesting the SMS read permission, keeping data minimisation intact (LINDDUN: identifiability). Confirm the code field is excluded from screenshots/telemetry payloads ({{SN-TEL-001}}).

## UX notes

Design reference: `screens-and-flows.md` §3 Login. Keep the six-cell visual; announce 'One-time code, 6 digits' as the field label, and place the resend affordance in the focus order immediately after the field. Errors appear as an announced toast plus inline text, per §10.

## Test plan

`app/test/features/auth/otp_accessibility_test.dart` (paste distributes and submits; autofill hints present; no paste blocking); integration test driving sign-in with the software keyboard disabled; manual matrix with VoiceOver + iOS QuickType, TalkBack + Autofill, NVDA + Chrome. Add a row to the audit matrix in {{SN-A11Y-017}}.

## Dependencies

{{SN-AUTH-006}}, {{SN-ONB-003}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Build the accessible status-message announcer (WCAG 4.1.3)
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §3.3 lists transient announcements ('Saved', 'Converted to text', 'Deleted N strokes', 'Recording saved', 'Page 3 of 12', 'Link copied', 'Pro trial started') and §10 requires the search result count to be a live region, but no issue owns **WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA)** as a system. Today each feature would call `SemanticsService.announce` ad hoc, which produces three failure modes we have already seen in comparable apps: announcements that steal focus, duplicate announcements when a provider rebuilds, and critical status (sync failure, recognition finished, upload progress) that is never announced at all because it renders as a passive chip rather than a toast.

## Scope

**In:** a single `SaneAnnouncer` service in `packages/sane_ui` with a typed API (`polite`, `assertive`, `progress(id, percent)`) that: routes to `SemanticsService.announce` with the correct `TextDirection` for the active locale; on web maps politeness to an `aria-live` region rather than relying on Flutter's default; de-duplicates identical messages inside a 1 s window; queues assertive over polite; never moves focus; suppresses announcements while a screen reader is not running to avoid wasted work; and throttles progress to at most one announcement every 5 s or 10 %. Wiring for every status surface that exists by M1 (save state, undo/redo results, page change, tool change, toast {{SN-DS-019}}) plus a registry so later features (search counts, sync state, recognition, upload/download progress, collaboration presence) attach without re-inventing the plumbing. A lint/checklist entry requiring any new passive status UI to register an announcement.

**Out:** the toast visual component ({{SN-DS-019}}); per-component name/role/state semantics and the toast-mirroring convention, which {{SN-A11Y-002}} owns and which this issue turns into one enforced service; per-feature copy, which each feature issue owns; audio captions ({{SN-A11Y-015}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every visual status change that is not itself focused produces exactly one announcement with the right politeness; verified by a semantics test harness that records announcements.
- [ ] Announcements never change focus; the focused control before and after is identical.
- [ ] Identical messages fired twice within 1 s announce once; progress announcements are throttled.
- [ ] On web the live region exists in the DOM with `aria-live="polite"`/`"assertive"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, verified by an axe/Playwright assertion.
- [ ] Announcement text is localised and bidi-safe (uses the active locale's text direction).
- [ ] A documented rule in `CONTRIBUTING.md` + the PR checklist: new status UI must call the announcer.

## Technical notes

`packages/sane_ui/lib/src/a11y/announcer.dart`, exposed through a Riverpod provider so tests can inject a recorder. Web needs a small `dart:html`/`package:web` shim appending a visually-hidden live region to the host document, because Flutter web's semantics overlay does not always surface `announce`. Read `MediaQuery.accessibleNavigation` to decide whether a screen reader is active. Keep messages in ARB ({{SN-I18N-002}}) with ICU plurals for 'Deleted {count} strokes'.

## Security & privacy

Status text must never contain note content beyond what is already on screen, and never secrets (share tokens, codes). Announcements are not logged or sent to telemetry. Rate limiting also protects against a malicious document causing announcement flooding (a denial-of-service against AT users) when many objects change at once.

## UX notes

Mirrors the toast policy in `screens-and-flows.md` §16: 2.4 s dwell, non-interruptive, never the only signal. Reduce-motion does not change announcements. Copy follows the voice rules in `docs/design/ux-principles.md`.

## Test plan

`packages/sane_ui/test/a11y/announcer_test.dart` (politeness routing, dedupe window, throttle, direction); widget tests asserting announcements for save/page/tool changes; a Playwright assertion for the web live region; a manual VoiceOver/TalkBack pass on the editor.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-002}}, {{SN-DS-019}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Expose content language to assistive tech and speech (3.1.1, 3.1.2)
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §11 requires OCR transcripts to be announced to screen readers and §7 requires Read Aloud, but nothing records **which language** a piece of content is in. WCAG 2.2 **3.1.1 Language of Page (A)** and **3.1.2 Language of Parts (AA)** are both in scope and both are currently unowned. The consequence is concrete and severe for our India-priority users: a Hindi handwriting transcript announced by an English VoiceOver voice is unintelligible, and an Arabic transcript read with an English voice is worse than silence. The same metadata drives Read Aloud voice selection in reading mode ({{SN-A11Y-014}}), the correct hyphenation/line-breaking, and correct font fallback ({{SN-I18N-008}}).

## Scope

**In:** a `languageTag` (BCP-47) on typed-text blocks, ink stroke groups (from the recognition language used, {{SN-I18N-010}}), images with alt text, audio transcripts, and the page as a whole (dominant language); propagation of that tag into the semantics layer (`Semantics(attributedLabel/localeIdentifier)` on iOS via `accessibilitySpeechLanguage`, Android `AccessibilityNodeInfo` extras / `LocaleSpan` on the content description, and `lang`/`dir` attributes on the web parallel DOM nodes and the document root); a documented fallback chain (object language → page language → notebook language → UI locale); Read Aloud voice selection keyed to the tag with a graceful fallback and an announced notice when no voice for that language is installed.

**Out:** translation ({{SN-HWR-022}}), automatic language detection quality beyond the recogniser's own output, per-word language switching inside a single ink block.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every accessible node exposes a language tag; the web parallel DOM carries `lang` and, for RTL content, `dir`.
- [ ] A Devanagari transcript is spoken with a Hindi voice by VoiceOver and TalkBack on a device with that voice installed.
- [ ] The document/root language follows the UI locale and updates live when the locale changes ({{SN-I18N-011}}).
- [ ] Read Aloud picks the content-language voice; if unavailable it falls back, announces the fallback once, and links to the OS voice-download setting.
- [ ] Mixed-language pages announce each block in its own language, verified on a page containing English + Hindi + Arabic blocks.
- [ ] The tag is persisted in the document model and survives sync, export and import round-trips.

## Technical notes

Add the field in `packages/sane_core` document model (a CRDT-safe scalar per object, defaulting to null = inherit). Platform channels: iOS `NSAttributedString` with `.accessibilitySpeechLanguage`; Android `SpannableString` with `LocaleSpan`; web via the parallel DOM node attributes built in {{SN-WEB-021}}. Flutter's `Semantics(attributedLabel:)` accepts locale-bearing attributed strings on iOS; where the framework cannot express it, use the platform channel already added for the custom rotor in {{SN-A11Y-004}}.

## Security & privacy

Language is content-derived metadata: keep it inside the encrypted document envelope like any other content field ({{SN-CRY-001}}), never in cleartext filenames or sync metadata, since a language list is a sensitive inference about the user (LINDDUN: disclosure/identifiability). No network lookup for language detection.

## UX notes

Invisible by default. The notebook language is shown (and overridable) in notebook settings next to the handwriting-recognition language; reading mode shows the detected language with a one-tap override.

## Test plan

`packages/sane_core/test/document/language_tag_test.dart` (inheritance chain, persistence, round-trip); semantics golden per platform asserting the emitted language; a manual multi-language announcement matrix with VoiceOver/TalkBack/NVDA; Read Aloud fallback test with the voice uninstalled.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-004}}, {{SN-I18N-010}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Let screen-reader users draw with direct-touch passthrough on the canvas
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §3 builds a parallel accessible tree so a screen-reader user can **read** the canvas, and §8 notes that freehand drawing is exempt from keyboard operability as an essential analog gesture. What neither the design doc nor any existing issue covers is the inverse problem: **with VoiceOver or TalkBack running, touches on the canvas are intercepted by the screen reader for exploration, so a blind or low-vision user cannot draw at all.** Both platforms solve this with an explicit opt-in region — iOS `UIAccessibilityTraits.allowsDirectInteraction` / `accessibilityDirectTouchOptions` (`.silentOnTouch`, `.requiresActivation`), Android `AccessibilityService`-honoured touch-exploration passthrough via `setTouchExplorationPassthroughRegion` and `FLAG_SERVICE_HANDLES_DOUBLE_TAP` semantics on the view. Without this, a user with residual vision or one drawing a signature, diagram, or maths working cannot use the core product while their screen reader is on.

## Scope

**In:** a **Direct drawing mode** on the canvas that, when enabled, marks the canvas rect as a direct-touch area so pen and finger input reaches the ink pipeline unmodified while the screen reader stays active for the rest of the chrome; an explicit toggle reachable from the editor toolbar and via a screen-reader custom action on the canvas node ('Start direct drawing' / 'Stop direct drawing'); an entry and exit announcement stating what changed and how to leave; automatic exit on tool change, overlay open, or app background; the iOS `requiresActivation` option so a single tap activates rather than draws accidentally; Android passthrough region kept in sync with the canvas bounds through a platform view/channel; on foldables and split view, recomputing the region when the window geometry changes.

**Out:** the parallel a11y tree itself ({{SN-A11Y-003}}), object custom actions ({{SN-A11Y-004}}), web (where the pointer is not intercepted the same way; keyboard placement covers it via {{SN-A11Y-008}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With VoiceOver running, enabling direct drawing lets a stroke be drawn on the canvas; the rest of the app remains VoiceOver-navigable.
- [ ] With TalkBack running, the canvas region is passed through and the same holds.
- [ ] Entering and leaving are announced, and a hint states the exit gesture/control; the mode never becomes a trap (a two-finger or explicit control always exits).
- [ ] The mode exits automatically on overlay open, tool change, backgrounding, and window-size change, with an announcement.
- [ ] Direct-touch regions follow the canvas rect within one frame after a layout change (split view, rotation, dock move).
- [ ] The toggle state is announced as a switch with its value and persists per profile.

## Technical notes

iOS: set the traits on the `UIView` hosting the Flutter canvas through `plugins/sane_ml_native`-style platform code or a dedicated `sane_a11y_native` channel; `accessibilityDirectTouchOptions` requires iOS 17+, so fall back to `allowsDirectInteraction` alone. Android: call `AccessibilityManager`-adjacent APIs on the host `View` (`setTouchExplorationPassthroughRegion` is an `AccessibilityService` API, so use `AccessibilityNodeInfo` direct-touch semantics plus `setAccessibilityDelegate` marking the region non-explorable and forwarding events) — record the chosen approach in an ADR if it deviates. Region maths must use the same viewport transform as {{SN-A11Y-003}}.

## Security & privacy

None beyond baseline; the mode changes only input routing. Ensure the toggle cannot be set by a deep link or shared document (no document-controlled a11y state), and that leaving the mode is always locally initiated.

## UX notes

Toolbar affordance sits with the other assistive controls; copy: 'Direct drawing — screen reader gestures pause over the canvas'. Pair with the motor-assist presets ({{SN-A11Y-013}}) in Settings so assistive users find it in one place.

## Test plan

Platform unit tests for region computation; `app/integration_test/a11y/direct_touch_test.dart` driving layout changes and asserting region updates; manual scripted runs with VoiceOver (iPad + iPhone) and TalkBack (tablet + foldable) drawing a stroke, exiting, and navigating away. Add rows to the {{SN-A11Y-017}} audit matrix.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-003}}, {{SN-ED-001}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Verify braille display output and rotor navigation for note content
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §13 requires end-to-end verification with VoiceOver, TalkBack and a desktop screen reader, and the Apple Accessibility Nutrition Label for VoiceOver explicitly covers **braille** output, yet no issue mentions braille displays or verifies what a refreshable braille user actually reads. Braille exposes problems speech hides: labels that are acceptable when spoken become unusable at 40 cells ('Pen tool, button, selected, double-tap to activate, page 3 of 12' scrolls for a minute); emoji and decorative glyphs in labels render as long braille words; announcements without a role are indistinguishable from content; and our OCR transcripts — potentially hundreds of characters per stroke group — flood the display with no structure.

## Scope

**In:** a braille-and-rotor verification pass over the shipped surfaces (editor chrome, tool palette, page rail, library, search, reading mode, audio transcript) using a refreshable display with VoiceOver (iPadOS braille screen input included) and TalkBack with BRLTTY, plus NVDA braille on web; a written **label-brevity standard** in `docs/design/accessibility.md` (name first, role from the platform, state as a value, no punctuation padding, no emoji in labels, transcripts truncated with a 'read full transcript' action); fixes to any label that violates it; verification that the custom rotor / reading controls from {{SN-A11Y-004}} expose headings, images, handwriting blocks and audio anchors, and that TalkBack reading controls (headings, controls, links) work on the same content; a regression golden capturing the semantics label text so brevity regressions surface in review.

**Out:** braille maths (Nemeth) for recognised equations — record as a follow-up; hardware procurement, which the maintainer arranges.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every interactive label fits within 40 braille cells or degrades gracefully (most important words first); the standard is documented and violations are fixed.
- [ ] No label contains emoji, decorative punctuation, or the word 'button'/'image' duplicated by the platform role.
- [ ] Long OCR transcripts are truncated in the node label with a custom action to read the full transcript in reading mode.
- [ ] The custom rotor / reading controls navigate between object types on iPadOS and Android, and NVDA element lists show the web parallel DOM objects with meaningful names.
- [ ] A scripted common-task flow (open notebook, find a handwriting block, convert to text, export) is completed using braille display only, and the session notes are attached to the issue.
- [ ] Semantics-label goldens are added so a label-length regression fails CI.

## Technical notes

Reuse the semantics snapshot harness from {{SN-A11Y-016}}; add a `maxLabelLength` assertion. Braille output derives from the same accessibility label, so no separate API is needed — the work is content discipline plus rotor correctness. On web, verify the parallel DOM nodes from {{SN-WEB-021}} have unique accessible names (NVDA element list shows duplicates plainly).

## Security & privacy

Braille session notes may contain note content; keep test artefacts in the private engagement folder, use synthetic fixture documents ({{SN-QA-011}}), and never attach real user content to the issue.

## UX notes

The brevity rules affect visible tooltips too (same strings); keep the visible label and the accessible name identical so Voice Control ({{SN-A11Y-010}}) keeps working.

## Test plan

This issue is itself a verification task; deliverables are the documented standard, the label fixes with unit coverage, the semantics goldens in `app/test/a11y/semantics_labels_golden_test.dart`, and a findings log feeding {{SN-A11Y-017}}.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-004}}, {{SN-GA11-002}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Honour Smart Invert, colour inversion and grayscale on ink, images and PDFs
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §4.2 requires a high-contrast variant for Increase Contrast and mentions colour inversion in passing, and the research source §4 says to test under Android colour correction and inversion. What no issue owns is the specific, well-known failure: **iOS Smart Invert and Android colour inversion invert photographs, PDFs and the ink canvas**, turning a scanned lecture handout into a negative and a user's black ink on white paper into white-on-black that no longer matches their intent or the exported artefact. Apple's remedy is `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors` on views that already handle dark presentation; Android has no direct equivalent, so the app must detect inversion-like settings and offer its own dark-paper treatment ({{SN-PDF-027}} already ships a PDF dark option we can route to).

## Scope

**In:** marking the ink canvas, page thumbnails, inserted images, stickers, PDF page renders, notebook covers and the mascot artwork as inversion-ignoring on iOS/iPadOS; a detection path for Android colour inversion / colour correction (via the platform channel already used for a11y settings in {{SN-A11Y-007}}) that, when on, suggests the app's own dark-paper mode once (dismissible, remembered) rather than fighting the OS filter; verification that the 17 looks remain legible under grayscale and under deuteranopia/protanopia colour correction, with fixes routed to the adjusted tokens ({{SN-DS-006}}); a documented rule in `docs/design/design-system.md` that any new full-bleed content surface must be added to the inversion-ignore list.

**Out:** the high-contrast variant ({{SN-A11Y-007}}), the colour-blind ink palette ({{SN-A11Y-011}}), PDF dark rendering itself ({{SN-PDF-027}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With Smart Invert on, the ink canvas, images, PDFs and covers render normally while chrome inverts; verified by screenshots on iPad and iPhone.
- [ ] With Android colour inversion on, content is legible and the app offers dark paper once, with the suggestion dismissible and remembered per profile.
- [ ] Under grayscale, no state (selected tool, recording, unread badge, sync status) is distinguishable by colour alone; failures are fixed at the token or component level.
- [ ] Under deuteranopia and protanopia simulation, subject colours and ink swatches remain distinguishable by name/shape; the simulation preview from {{SN-A11Y-011}} is used as the harness.
- [ ] A design-system rule and a PR-checklist line exist for new content surfaces.

## Technical notes

iOS: set `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors = true` on the platform view hosting the canvas and on image/PDF texture views; in Flutter this needs the host view, so extend the native surface plugin rather than the Dart widget tree. Android: there is no per-view opt-out; read `Settings.Secure.accessibility_display_inversion_enabled` and `accessibility_display_daltonizer_enabled` through the a11y settings channel. Grayscale/CVD verification can run offline over golden images with a colour-transform filter in `app/test/a11y/`.

## Security & privacy

Reading OS accessibility settings reveals disability-adjacent information: keep the values in memory only, never persist them to sync or telemetry, and gate any behavioural change behind local preferences (privacy-by-design; LINDDUN identifiability).

## UX notes

The Android suggestion is a one-time toast/sheet using existing components ({{SN-DS-019}}), copy: 'Dark paper may read better with colour inversion on.' Never auto-switch the user's look.

## Test plan

Golden tests applying invert/grayscale/CVD filters to representative screens across the offending looks (Pop, Glass, Cyberpunk, Neo-Brutalism light); `app/test/a11y/inversion_test.dart` for the settings channel and the one-time suggestion logic; manual device passes on iPadOS and Android 14+.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-007}}, {{SN-PDF-027}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Support OS magnification and 400% browser zoom without losing content
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §7 covers Dynamic Type and 200% text scaling and §2 covers reflow at 320 CSS px, but the research source §4 also requires that layouts 'remain usable when magnified', and WCAG **1.4.10 Reflow** is measured at **400% browser zoom** on a 1280 px viewport — not only at a narrow window. Screen magnification is a different failure mode from text scaling: the viewport does not change, so our sticky toolbars, floating palette dock, and full-screen overlays can cover the magnified focus, and the magnifier follows the caret/focus only if we keep the focused element on screen and report caret rects correctly. Low-vision users are our second-largest assistive group after screen-reader users, and magnification is how most of them work.

## Scope

**In:** an audit-and-fix pass for OS magnification (iPadOS Zoom, Android magnification, macOS/Windows screen magnifiers on web) and 400% browser zoom; guaranteeing the focused control and the text caret are scrolled into view on every focus change so the magnifier follows; ensuring chrome that is pinned (palette dock, page rail, audio bar, toast) never permanently covers the focus rect — collapsing or auto-hiding when the focused element would be obscured (WCAG 2.4.11); exposing caret rects to the platform (`TextInputClient` caret reporting on native, correct DOM caret on web) so system magnifiers track typing; verifying at 400% zoom on a 1280x1024 viewport that no content is lost and no two-dimensional scrolling appears outside the explicitly allowed canvas; fixing any fixed-height container that clips at high zoom.

**Out:** the app's own zoom window ({{SN-ED-019}}) and the canvas viewport zoom ({{SN-PG-001}}), text scaling ({{SN-A11Y-005}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At 400% browser zoom on 1280x1024, every screen reflows to a single column with no loss of content or function and no horizontal page scroll (canvas, tables and code excepted, each in its own scroll container).
- [ ] Focus changes scroll the focused control fully into view; the focus rect is never fully covered by the dock, rail, audio bar or toast.
- [ ] The system magnifier follows the caret while typing in note titles, search, and typed text on iPadOS, Android and web.
- [ ] With iPadOS Zoom at 5x and Android magnification at 4x, a scripted flow (open notebook, pick a tool, write, convert to text, export) is completable; findings are logged and fixed.
- [ ] No container clips its content at 200% text x 400% zoom in the golden matrix.

## Technical notes

Use `Scrollable.ensureVisible` on focus change via a `FocusManager` listener in the app shell; collapse the dock via the existing adaptive-layout primitives ({{SN-DS-026}}) using window-size class plus an effective-viewport calculation (device pixel ratio x text scale x zoom). On web, verify Flutter's viewport reacts to browser zoom (it changes `devicePixelRatio`, not `MediaQuery.size`) — this is a known Flutter-web trap and may need a `window.visualViewport` listener.

## Security & privacy

None beyond baseline. Do not persist or transmit the detected zoom level (an assistive-need signal) to telemetry.

## UX notes

When chrome auto-collapses because of focus obstruction, it returns on the next focus move; never animate it under reduce motion ({{SN-A11Y-006}}). Reference `screens-and-flows.md` §7 for dock/rail placement.

## Test plan

Playwright runs at 400% zoom asserting no horizontal overflow and single-column reflow; widget tests for the ensure-visible and obstruction-collapse logic; golden matrix at 200% text; manual magnifier passes on iPadOS/Android. Add rows to the {{SN-A11Y-017}} matrix.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-005}}, {{SN-DS-026}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Verify flash safety and cap photosensitive motion (WCAG 2.3.1)
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §2 asserts that nothing flashes more than 3 times per second ('the recording dot pulses well under'), and §13 lists it in the acceptance checklist, but that assertion is currently an unverified claim. **WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (A)** is a seizure-safety criterion, not a polish item: getting it wrong can physically harm a photosensitive user. We ship motion in several places that can compound — the recording pulse, the audio waveform, loading skeleton shimmer ({{SN-DS-022}}), dock edge-glow, brush fly-ins, page-turn, ink replay, the Cyberpunk and Y2K looks' accent treatments, and any confetti/celebration in onboarding or study streaks. Nobody has measured the combined luminance change per second, and no gate stops a future animation from crossing the threshold.

## Scope

**In:** an inventory of every animation in the app with its frequency, luminance delta and area (the WCAG general/red flash thresholds care about area > 25 % of a 10-degree field and luminance change > 10 %); measurement of the worst candidates by rendering the animation offscreen and computing per-frame relative luminance in a test harness; fixes where anything approaches 3 Hz or the flash area threshold (slow it, reduce contrast delta, or make it a static state); an automated **flash-safety test** that runs the motion tokens ({{SN-DS-025}}) and a set of scripted animations through the luminance analyser and fails CI above threshold; a rule in `docs/design/ux-principles.md` and the PR checklist ({{SN-A11Y-019}}) that new animations declare frequency and luminance delta.

**Out:** reduce-motion behaviour ({{SN-A11Y-006}}), user-drawn content (a user animating their own ink is content, not chrome), video content ({{SN-GA11-013}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An inventory table exists in `docs/design/accessibility.md` (or an appendix) listing each animation, its frequency, area and measured luminance delta.
- [ ] No app-authored animation exceeds 3 flashes per second, and none combines > 25 % screen area with > 10 % relative luminance change at any frequency above 1 Hz.
- [ ] The recording indicator, skeleton shimmer, and the Cyberpunk/Y2K accent treatments are explicitly measured and pass.
- [ ] An automated analyser test runs in CI over a set of rendered animation frame sequences and fails on a violation.
- [ ] The PR checklist requires a frequency/luminance declaration for new motion.
- [ ] Any celebration/confetti effect is capped and disabled under reduce motion.

## Technical notes

Harness in `app/test/a11y/flash_safety_test.dart`: drive a widget with a controlled `Ticker`, capture frames via `TestWidgetsFlutterBinding` image capture, compute WCAG relative luminance per frame over the changing region, and assert transitions per second. Relative luminance code can be shared with the contrast checker from {{SN-DS-007}}.

## Security & privacy

None beyond baseline; test artefacts use synthetic fixtures. Note the safety framing in the conformance statement ({{SN-A11Y-018}}) so the claim is evidence-backed rather than asserted.

## UX notes

Where a pulse must slow, prefer a static state plus a text label (motion must never be the only signal, per §6). Keep the recording indicator unmistakable: steady red dot + 'Recording' label is already the reduce-motion behaviour and may simply become the default.

## Test plan

The analyser test above; golden frame sequences for the five highest-risk animations; a manual review of any look whose accent produces high-contrast strobing; results recorded in the {{SN-A11Y-017}} audit matrix.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-006}}, {{SN-DS-025}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Make time limits adjustable: OTP expiry, app lock and toast dwell
body:
## Context

WCAG **2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (A)** and **2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A)** are absent from `docs/design/accessibility.md` §2 and from every issue, yet the product has at least four timed behaviours that affect users who read slowly, use a screen reader, or type with a switch: the **OTP expiry window** ({{SN-AUTH-006}}), the **biometric/PIN app-lock idle timeout** ({{SN-AUTH-014}}), the **2.4 s toast dwell** ({{SN-DS-019}}) which is the only carrier of several status messages, and any auto-advancing tip/onboarding carousel ({{SN-ONB-005}}, {{SN-ONB-010}}). A screen-reader user can easily miss a 2.4 s toast entirely; a switch user may not finish typing an OTP before it expires. 2.2.1 permits security exceptions for the code lifetime itself, but it still requires a warning, an easy extension, and a re-issue path.

## Scope

**In:** a **status history** surface so any toast can be re-read after it disappears (a 'Recent messages' item in the app menu plus an announced live-region message, the standard 2.2.2 remedy for transient content); toast dwell that scales with the OS text-scale and with `MediaQuery.accessibleNavigation` (longer when a screen reader is active) and never auto-dismisses a toast carrying an error; a visible, announced OTP countdown with a one-tap resend and a documented security-exception note; an app-lock idle timeout that is user-configurable (30 s / 1 min / 5 min / 15 min / never-while-active) with a warning before locking and a grace period that does not lose work; pausing auto-advancing carousels on focus/hover and under reduce motion; a rule that no timed interaction may destroy user data.

**Out:** the OTP transport and rate limits ({{SN-AUTH-006}}), session token lifetimes on the server ({{SN-AUTH-002}}), autosave cadence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every toast is recoverable from a status history for at least the session; the history is keyboard and screen-reader reachable.
- [ ] Toast dwell is at least 2.4 s, scales with text scale, extends when a screen reader is active, and error toasts require dismissal.
- [ ] The OTP screen shows and announces the remaining time and offers resend; expiry produces a clear, announced message and never a silent failure.
- [ ] App-lock timeout is configurable in Settings (Security), with a pre-lock warning and no data loss on lock.
- [ ] Auto-advancing content pauses on focus, on hover, and when reduce motion is set.
- [ ] The security exception for the OTP lifetime is documented in `docs/design/accessibility-conformance.md`.

## Technical notes

Status history is a ring buffer fed by the announcer ({{SN-GA11-002}}) — one source of truth for visual toast and announcement. App-lock timeout lives in the per-profile preference store ({{SN-SET-003}}) and is enforced by {{SN-AUTH-014}}; the setting row belongs in the Security tab ({{SN-SET-013}}).

## Security & privacy

Lengthening the app-lock timeout weakens shoulder-surfing/device-theft protection: cap the maximum, keep the default short, and require re-auth for destructive or export actions regardless of the timer. The status history must never contain secrets (share tokens, OTPs) — enforce by construction in the announcer API and cover with a test. Document the residual risk in the threat model ({{SN-SEC-001}}).

## UX notes

`screens-and-flows.md` §16 (toast) and §12 (Settings). The status history uses an existing list surface; entries carry a relative timestamp formatted through {{SN-I18N-005}}.

## Test plan

`app/test/a11y/timing_test.dart` (dwell scaling, error toasts persist, history capture, no secrets in history); `app/test/features/auth/otp_countdown_test.dart`; integration test for lock warning and resume; manual screen-reader pass confirming toasts are re-readable.

## Dependencies

{{SN-AUTH-006}}, {{SN-AUTH-014}}, {{SN-DS-019}}, {{SN-GA11-002}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Add accessible error prevention and recovery for destructive actions
body:
## Context

WCAG **3.3.1 Error Identification**, **3.3.3 Error Suggestion** and **3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)** are not in the `accessibility.md` §2 matrix and no issue owns them, yet 3.3.4 applies directly to three flows we ship: **account and data deletion** ({{SN-AUTH-018}}), **purchases and plan changes** ({{SN-BILL-001}}), and any action that deletes user data irreversibly (empty trash, delete notebook, remove a page, revoke a share link that others depend on). 3.3.4 requires such actions to be reversible, checked, or confirmed — and the confirmation must itself be accessible: announced, keyboard-operable, with the consequence stated in text rather than implied by a red button (1.4.1). Our current design relies on colour-coded destructive styling plus a dialog whose copy has not been specified for AT.

## Scope

**In:** a single `DestructiveActionGuard` pattern used by every irreversible action: a dialog stating in plain text **what** will be deleted, **how many** items, whether it is recoverable and for how long, with the confirm control labelled by the action ('Delete 12 pages') rather than 'OK'; focus moved to the dialog and returned to the invoker on cancel, no focus trap, Escape cancels; an announced result; an **undo window** where technically possible (trash/restore for notebooks and pages) and an explicit 'this cannot be undone' sentence where not; typed confirmation only where the consequence is account-level; accessible error handling across all forms — errors announced, associated with the field programmatically, described in text with a concrete correction suggestion, and never signalled by colour alone; preserving user input after an error so nothing must be retyped.

**Out:** billing checkout UI ({{SN-BILL-001}}) beyond adopting this pattern, share-link revocation semantics ({{SN-SHR-018}}), the trash data model ({{SN-LIB-001}}).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every irreversible action routes through the guard; a test enumerates destructive call sites and fails if one bypasses it.
- [ ] Confirmation dialogs state item counts and recoverability in text; the confirm button names the action; colour is never the only destructive signal.
- [ ] Focus enters the dialog, is trapped only for the modal's lifetime, returns to the invoker on cancel, and Escape always cancels.
- [ ] Deletion results are announced through the announcer ({{SN-GA11-002}}) and, where recoverable, offer an undo action reachable by keyboard and AT within the undo window.
- [ ] Form errors are announced, programmatically associated with their field, and include a suggestion; user input is preserved.
- [ ] Account deletion requires an explicit typed confirmation and states the exact data scope and irreversibility.

## Technical notes

Implement in `packages/sane_ui` on top of the dialog component ({{SN-DS-019}}) with a typed `DestructiveAction { titleKey, bodyKey, itemCount, recoverableFor, requiresTypedConfirmation }`. Field-level error association uses `Semantics(label/hint)` plus `aria-describedby` on web. Enumerate destructive call sites with a Semgrep rule under `tools/semgrep/a11y.yml` ({{SN-A11Y-019}}).

## Security & privacy

Account deletion is a GDPR/DPDP right-to-erasure flow ({{SN-PRV-001}}): the confirmation must state scope accurately (local data, synced copies in the user's own drive, shared copies that cannot be recalled). Guard against clickjacking-style accidental confirmation by requiring an explicit press, not a drag or gesture. Do not weaken re-authentication requirements for destructive actions to make them easier.

## UX notes

Copy follows `docs/design/ux-principles.md` (plain language, no euphemism). Dialog layouts must survive 200% text and 320 px width ({{SN-A11Y-005}}).

## Test plan

`app/test/a11y/destructive_guard_test.dart` (focus entry/return, Escape, labels, announcements, undo path); a Semgrep test proving bypasses are caught; integration tests for notebook delete/restore and account deletion; manual screen-reader confirmation of each dialog.

## Dependencies

{{SN-AUTH-018}}, {{SN-LIB-001}}, {{SN-GA11-002}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Provide Consistent Help and eliminate redundant entry (3.2.6, 3.3.7)
body:
## Context

WCAG 2.2 added two AA criteria aimed at cognitive accessibility that `docs/design/accessibility.md` §2 does not list and no issue owns: **3.2.6 Consistent Help** (if a help mechanism is available on multiple screens, it appears in the same relative order/location on each) and **3.3.7 Redundant Entry** (information the user already provided in the same process is auto-populated or available to select, rather than re-entered). Both matter most for the users we most want to serve — students onboarding on a phone, users with memory or attention differences, and switch/voice users for whom every extra input is expensive. We currently have help in at least three places (onboarding tips {{SN-ONB-010}}, Settings About/Help {{SN-SET-015}}, the in-app help centre {{SN-DOC-010}}) with no rule about placement, and several flows re-ask for information (subjects chosen in onboarding vs. first notebook creation; display name at profile creation vs. share invitations; email at sign-in vs. student verification).

## Scope

**In:** a documented **help placement rule** — the help entry point occupies the same relative position (end of the top bar / last item in the overflow menu / final row of any settings section) on every screen that offers it — and an audit that moves any deviation; a single help affordance component so placement is enforced by construction; an inventory of every multi-step process that asks for the same data twice (onboarding to first notebook, sign-in to student verification, share invite to collaborator name, billing address if any) with auto-population or a pick-from-previous control for each; a rule that re-entry is required only where a security control demands it (password/OTP re-entry is explicitly exempt under 3.3.7).

**Out:** help content authoring ({{SN-DOC-008}}), the help centre implementation ({{SN-DOC-010}}), onboarding flow redesign.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every screen that offers help uses the shared affordance in the documented position; a widget test enumerates screens and asserts placement.
- [ ] An inventory table of redundant-entry points exists, each resolved by auto-population, a select-from-previous control, or a documented security exemption.
- [ ] Subjects chosen during onboarding pre-fill the first notebook creation; the profile display name pre-fills share invitations; the signed-in email pre-fills verification forms.
- [ ] Auto-populated values are announced as such and are editable; nothing is silently submitted on the user's behalf.
- [ ] The help affordance is keyboard reachable, labelled, and does not move between screens of the same class.
- [ ] The conformance statement ({{SN-A11Y-018}}) records 3.2.6 and 3.3.7 as supported with evidence.

## Technical notes

Help affordance in `packages/sane_ui` (`SaneHelpAction`) inserted by the app shell rather than by each screen, so position is structural. Redundant-entry plumbing reads from the per-profile preference store ({{SN-SET-003}}) and the identity profile ({{SN-AUTH-007}}); values are passed as initial form state, never as hidden fields.

## Security & privacy

Auto-population must not leak data across profiles ({{SN-AUTH-013}}) or from a signed-in account into guest mode ({{SN-AUTH-010}}); source the values from the active profile only. Never auto-populate credentials, OTPs, or payment details from app state — those belong to the platform autofill/keychain ({{SN-GA11-001}}).

## UX notes

Pre-filled fields show a subtle 'from your profile' hint and remain fully editable. Help copy and iconography follow `docs/design/component-inventory.md`.

## Test plan

`app/test/a11y/consistent_help_test.dart` (placement across screens); `app/test/features/onboarding/redundant_entry_test.dart` (pre-fill correctness, profile isolation, editability); a manual pass of the two longest flows with a switch device.

## Dependencies

{{SN-DOC-010}}, {{SN-SET-015}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Export tagged, accessible PDFs with structure, reading order and alt text
body:
## Context

{{SN-SHR-012}} preserves alt-text and OCR transcripts as metadata in exports and {{SN-PDF-020}} embeds an invisible OCR text layer so exported handwriting is searchable, but neither produces a **tagged** PDF. An untagged PDF with an invisible text layer is searchable yet still inaccessible: screen readers get no structure, no reading order, no headings, no alt text on images, no language, and no table semantics — exactly the complaint students make about lecture handouts. PDF is the format our users hand to classmates, professors and accessibility offices, and in the EU the European Accessibility Act treats documents distributed by a service as part of that service. Shipping tagged PDF/UA-oriented export is both a conformance requirement and a genuine differentiator: no major handwriting-notes competitor exports tagged PDFs.

## Scope

**In:** a tagged-PDF writer in `packages/sane_pdf` that emits a `/StructTreeRoot` with `/Document`, `/H1..H3`, `/P`, `/Figure`, `/Table`, `/L`/`/LI` elements; mapping from the document model — typed text blocks to paragraphs/headings/lists, recognised ink headings to headings, handwriting stroke groups to `/Figure` with the OCR transcript as `/Alt` (plus the invisible text layer from {{SN-PDF-020}} inside the figure so search still works), images to `/Figure` with user/AI alt text, shapes to `/Figure` with the recognised name, audio anchors to annotations with contents text; document-level metadata: `/Lang` from {{SN-GA11-003}}, `/Title` from the notebook name, `/DisplayDocTitle` true, and the `/MarkInfo /Marked true` flag; a reading-order pass ordering structure elements by the page's logical order rather than draw order; artifacts marked for decorative strokes and paper patterns so AT skips them.

**Out:** full PDF/UA-1 certification and a Matterhorn-protocol audit (record as a follow-up), annotation round-trip ({{SN-PDF-016}}), the flattening path ({{SN-PDF-019}}) which keeps its current behaviour with tags added.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Exported PDFs open in Acrobat/veraPDF with a populated tag tree, marked content, document language and display-document-title set.
- [ ] A page of handwriting exports as a figure whose alt text is the OCR transcript; images carry their alt text; decorative paper is marked as an artifact.
- [ ] Reading order matches the page's logical order (verified against a fixture with two columns and an inserted image) and is read correctly by NVDA and VoiceOver in Preview.
- [ ] veraPDF (or an equivalent checker) runs in CI over fixture exports and reports zero structural/tagging errors of the categories we claim to support.
- [ ] Tagging adds no more than 15 % to export time for a 100-page notebook and does not change visual output byte-for-byte in a pixel comparison.
- [ ] The exported file's accessibility properties are documented in the help centre and the conformance statement.

## Technical notes

Extend the exporter behind {{SN-SHR-003}}; the structure tree must be built alongside content streams with `/BDC`/`/EMC` marked-content operators, so the page painter needs a tagging-aware wrapper. Keep the tag builder pure and unit-testable over the document model. Run veraPDF in CI via a container step in `devsecops.yml`.

## Security & privacy

Tags carry transcript text: if the export is redacted or a page range is chosen, the tag tree must be filtered identically or it leaks content outside the selection — cover with a test. Alt text may contain personal content, so honour the same export-consent and share defaults as {{SN-SHR-020}}. Never embed profile identifiers, device names or telemetry IDs in PDF metadata.

## UX notes

Export sheet gains an 'Accessible (tagged) PDF' note rather than a toggle — tagging is always on; if the user picks flattened image export, state plainly that tags and text are not included.

## Test plan

`packages/sane_pdf/test/export/tagged_pdf_test.dart` (tag tree shape per fixture, alt text presence, artifact marking, page-range filtering); a veraPDF CI job over three fixtures; manual NVDA + VoiceOver reading of an exported notebook; performance test on the 100-page fixture ({{SN-PDF-026}} harness).

## Dependencies

{{SN-SHR-003}}, {{SN-SHR-012}}, {{SN-PDF-020}}, {{SN-GA11-003}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Caption, transcribe and audio-describe every product video
body:
## Context

`docs/design/accessibility.md` §12 commits us to truthfully declaring the Apple Accessibility Nutrition Label for **Captions**, and the research source §12 lists **Audio Descriptions** as the ninth declarable feature. {{SN-A11Y-015}} covers captions for the user's own audio recordings, but nothing covers **our** media: App Store and Play store preview videos, the marketing site's hero and feature videos ({{SN-SITE-003}}, {{SN-SITE-004}}), help-centre how-to videos or GIFs ({{SN-DOC-010}}), onboarding motion, and any launch/social video. WCAG 1.2.1–1.2.5 apply: prerecorded audio needs a transcript, prerecorded video with audio needs captions (1.2.2, A) and audio description (1.2.5, AA). Store review has also begun checking that declared labels match shipped behaviour, so an uncaptioned preview video makes a declared label false.

## Scope

**In:** an inventory of every video/animated asset we publish; a production standard requiring, for each: burned-in-safe open or closed captions (WebVTT for web, SRT/CC for stores), a text transcript published next to the asset, audio description either as a described variant or by designing narration that already describes on-screen action (the preferred, cheaper route), no flashing above threshold ({{SN-GA11-008}}), and localisation of caption files for the launch locales ({{SN-I18N-003}}); a decision and note for silent GIF/loop assets (they need a text alternative, not captions, and must be pausable per 2.2.2); wiring the web player to expose caption tracks, keyboard controls and a transcript toggle; a release-gate checklist line ({{SN-REL-013}}) blocking submission if a store preview video lacks captions in the primary locale.

**Out:** in-app recording captions ({{SN-A11Y-015}}); marketing copywriting; video production scheduling.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every published video asset has a caption file in the primary locale and a linked transcript; the inventory records both.
- [ ] Store preview videos carry captions (or are silent with on-screen text) and the App Store Captions label is declared only when this holds for all in-app media too.
- [ ] Audio description is provided or the narration is verified as self-describing by an explicit review note per asset.
- [ ] The website player exposes caption tracks, is fully keyboard operable, and offers a visible transcript; verified by axe and a manual NVDA pass ({{SN-SITE-015}}).
- [ ] Autoplaying or looping motion on the site and in help content can be paused and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- [ ] The release checklist blocks submission when the gate fails; the rule is documented.

## Technical notes

Store caption/transcript files in the repo next to the asset (`website/public/media/*.vtt`, help-centre content bundle) so they version with the video and can be localised through the same translation workflow as ARB strings ({{SN-I18N-012}}). The in-app help centre is offline-first ({{SN-DOC-010}}), so transcripts must ship in the bundle, not be fetched.

## Security & privacy

Media assets must be self-hosted with the website's no-third-party rule ({{SN-SITE-014}}) — no YouTube/Vimeo embeds, which would leak visitor IPs and add tracking. Transcripts must not contain real user content or personal data from demo recordings; use fixture notebooks.

## UX notes

Captions styled per the site design tokens with a >= 4.5:1 contrast over the video; transcript collapsible but present in the DOM for search and screen readers.

## Test plan

A CI check that every referenced video in the site/help bundle has a sibling caption file and transcript; Playwright assertions for player keyboard operation and caption track presence; manual review of each store preview before submission, logged in {{SN-REL-013}}.

## Dependencies

{{SN-REL-010}}, {{SN-SITE-015}}, {{SN-DOC-010}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Make keyboard shortcuts work on non-Latin layouts and during IME composition
body:
## Context

{{SN-A11Y-008}} and {{SN-ED-022}} give us single-key tool shortcuts (P/H/E/V/S/T/I/R) and a Cmd/Ctrl shortcut map, and {{SN-I18N-009}} requires that composition events are never intercepted. What neither owns is the interaction between the two: **a shortcut map defined by character produces the wrong key on a non-QWERTY physical layout and can be unreachable on a non-Latin one.** On AZERTY, the QWERTY 'A' position yields 'Q'; on a Devanagari, Hangul or Cyrillic layout, pressing the physical 'P' key produces a non-Latin character and a character-based matcher never fires, so the pen tool becomes unreachable by keyboard for exactly the users our India-priority locales target. Conversely, a physical-key matcher that ignores IME state will steal keystrokes mid-composition and corrupt typed Hindi, Japanese or Korean text. Keyboard operability is a WCAG 2.1.1 requirement, so this is an accessibility defect as much as an i18n one.

## Scope

**In:** converting the shortcut layer to match on **physical key codes** (`PhysicalKeyboardKey` / `KeyboardEvent.code`) for positional single-key tool shortcuts, while keeping **logical** matching for shortcuts users think of as characters (Cmd+Z, Cmd+C); suppressing all single-key shortcuts while a text field has focus or an IME composition is active (`TextInputClient.currentAutofillScope`/composing range, `KeyboardEvent.isComposing` on web, `compositionstart`/`compositionend`); a visible shortcut cheat sheet ({{SN-ED-022}}) that renders the **label of the physical key on the user's layout** rather than a hard-coded letter; verification on AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak, Devanagari InScript, Hangul 2-set, Japanese JIS and Pinyin layouts; a documented rule in `docs/design/gestures-and-shortcuts.md` stating which shortcuts are positional and which are logical.

**Out:** user-remappable shortcuts (backlog), the gesture map, on-screen keyboard behaviour on phones.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every single-key tool shortcut fires from the same physical key position on AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak, InScript, Hangul and JIS layouts.
- [ ] No shortcut fires while a text field is focused or while an IME composition is in progress; typed Hindi/Japanese/Korean text is never corrupted or truncated by a shortcut handler.
- [ ] Cmd/Ctrl combinations continue to match logically (Cmd+Z is undo regardless of layout).
- [ ] The cheat sheet displays the key label for the active layout, or the physical key name where the label is unavailable.
- [ ] An automated test drives synthetic key events for at least four layouts and asserts the resulting action.
- [ ] `gestures-and-shortcuts.md` documents the positional-vs-logical rule and the IME suppression rule.

## Technical notes

Flutter: prefer `ShortcutActivator` implementations keyed on `PhysicalKeyboardKey` and a custom activator that consults an `ImeCompositionNotifier`. On web, Flutter's key data already carries `physicalKey` derived from `event.code`; verify `isComposing` is respected in the engine path and add a guard if not. Key labels can come from `KeyboardLayoutMap` (`navigator.keyboard.getLayoutMap()`) on Chromium, with the physical key name as fallback elsewhere.

## Security & privacy

A keyboard-layout map is a fingerprinting signal: read it only for label rendering, never persist it, and never send it to telemetry ({{SN-TEL-001}}). Ensure the key handler cannot be driven by document content (a malicious shared note must not synthesise shortcuts).

## UX notes

Cheat sheet reference: `screens-and-flows.md` §7 and `gestures-and-shortcuts.md` §6. Where a label cannot be resolved, show the physical position name (for example 'key P position') rather than a misleading letter.

## Test plan

`app/test/features/editor/shortcuts_layout_test.dart` (synthetic events per layout, IME suppression, logical combos); `app/integration_test/i18n/ime_shortcut_test.dart` typing Hindi and Japanese into a text object with shortcuts bound; manual pass with a physical AZERTY keyboard and an InScript layout.

## Dependencies

{{SN-A11Y-008}}, {{SN-ED-022}}, {{SN-I18N-009}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
- [ ] Reviewed against docs/security/secure-coding-checklist.md

title: Isolate bidirectional text and localise digits in interpolated strings
body:
## Context

{{SN-I18N-007}} mirrors chrome for RTL locales and {{SN-I18N-002}} sets up ARB messages, but neither handles what happens when **user content of one direction is interpolated into a UI string of another** — which is most of our chrome: 'Delete {notebook}?', '{name} shared {notebook}', 'match: {snippet}', 'page {n} of {m}', file names in export toasts, tags, and collaborator names. Without explicit isolation, the Unicode bidi algorithm lets an Arabic notebook title reorder the surrounding English sentence (and vice versa), producing text that reads as a different sentence — a legibility bug and a spoofing vector, since RLO/LRO override characters in a shared note title or a collaborator's display name can visually reverse a destructive confirmation ('Delete' rendered after the name) or disguise a file extension. Accessibility is affected too: screen readers announce isolated runs with the right direction and voice.

## Scope

**In:** a `SaneBidi` helper that wraps every interpolated user-supplied value in isolation marks (FSI...PDI, or `Directionality`/`Unicode.FSI` in Flutter text spans) at the formatting boundary, applied by default in the localisation accessor layer so callers cannot forget; stripping or neutralising the explicit override characters (U+202A..U+202E, U+2066..U+2069) from titles, names, tags and filenames on input and at render; digit shaping policy — decide and document that numbers in UI chrome use the locale's default digit set via `intl` ({{SN-I18N-005}}) and that user-entered digits are preserved as typed; verification that mixed-direction search result snippets highlight the correct range; correct `dir`/`textDirection` on web parallel-DOM nodes for content runs ({{SN-GA11-003}}).

**Out:** RTL chrome mirroring ({{SN-I18N-007}}), complex-script shaping ({{SN-TXT-007}}), the canvas, which is never mirrored.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every ARB message with a placeholder renders its value isolated; a lint/test fails if a placeholder is interpolated without isolation.
- [ ] An Arabic notebook title inside an English confirmation sentence renders in the correct order, verified by golden images in both directions.
- [ ] Explicit bidi override characters in titles, display names, tags and export filenames are removed or rendered inert; a fuzz test covers this.
- [ ] Search snippets with mixed direction highlight the matched term at the correct visual position.
- [ ] Numbers in chrome follow the locale digit set; user-typed digits are preserved verbatim in content.
- [ ] Screen readers announce each isolated run with its own direction (spot-checked with VoiceOver Arabic and TalkBack Hindi).

## Technical notes

Implement at `app/lib/l10n/` in a wrapper around `AppLocalizations` (or a generated extension) so every accessor isolates automatically; for `Text.rich` use `TextSpan`s carrying direction. Sanitisation belongs in the shared input-validation layer in `packages/sane_core` so sync, export and collaboration all inherit it. Export filenames additionally need path-safe normalisation ({{SN-SHR-002}}).

## Security & privacy

This is a spoofing control, not only a layout fix: bidi overrides in shared-note titles and collaborator display names ({{SN-COL-001}}) can mislead a user into confirming a destructive or sharing action (STRIDE: spoofing; OWASP A03 injection-adjacent). Cover the sanitiser with the fuzz corpus ({{SN-QA-013}}) and record the control in the threat model ({{SN-SEC-001}}).

## UX notes

No visible affordance; correctness only. Where a title is sanitised, keep the original bytes in storage and sanitise at render, so the user's own text is never silently rewritten.

## Test plan

`app/test/l10n/bidi_isolation_test.dart` (isolation applied, override stripping, digit policy); goldens for `ar` and `he`-style mixed strings across key screens; a fuzz case set in the shared corpus; manual screen-reader spot checks.

## Dependencies

{{SN-I18N-002}}, {{SN-I18N-007}}.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Code + tests merged, CI green (lint, analyze, unit, security scans)
- [ ] Docs/ADR updated if behaviour or architecture changed
